title: Living ashtpadi 12
hook: humility is the doorway to every virtue in Sukhmani

segments.voice: Yesterday, neechaa, and your line: lowest is highest. Did you do one thankless helpful thing? Today we close the twelfth ashtpadi by living it. Day four hundred eighty-five.

Two words, said badly or said well, can change a whole evening: I'm sorry. Most of us know exactly how hard they are. You rehearse them in the car. You add a but. You explain why it wasn't really your fault before you get to the part where it was. The apology gets stuck somewhere between the throat and the pride. And then, when someone finally says it plainly, no but, no speech, something in the room loosens. Sukhmani has spent a whole ashtpadi on why that loosening happens. Today: humility, put first.
screen: `I'M SORRY. TWO WORDS.` → `REHEARSED, STUCK, WITH A BUT.` → `SAID PLAINLY, THE ROOM LOOSENS.`

segments.voice: Look at where the twelfth ashtpadi sits. Sukhmani is twenty-four ashtpadis long, and this one lands near the middle of the hymn. Before it, Guru Arjan has talked about remembering the Name, about the company of the holy, about the One who does everything. Here he stops and names the thing all of that depends on. In the second stanza of this ashtpadi, he puts it this way, in paraphrase: as long as a person thinks, something gets done by me, there's no peace for them. As long as a person thinks, I am the doer, they keep going round and round. The I is the blockage. While it's in the doorway, nothing else can come through. That's why many Sikhs call humility the doorway to the other virtues. Guru Nanak had already said something like it in Asa di Var, a hymn sung in many gurdwaras every morning: sweetness and humility, Nanak, are the essence of all virtue and goodness. Mithat neevee, in Punjabi. Sweetness, and lowness. Notice the pair. Humility in Sikh teaching is never sour. It isn't a grim, hunched-over feeling of being nothing. It's sweet: easy to be around, quick to laugh, quick to say sorry. And that's the living part. An apology is humility in the smallest possible size. It says: I was the doer of this, and it wasn't right. Strangely, owning the mistake is the opposite of pride, because pride's whole job is to defend the self. So the twelfth ashtpadi lands somewhere very ordinary: a kitchen, a car, a group chat, wherever two people have just rubbed each other the wrong way. Humility first, and then everything else has room.
screen: `THE MIDDLE OF SUKHMANI.` · `WHILE I AM THE DOER, NO PEACE.` · `MITHAT NEEVEE: SWEET AND LOW.` · `SORRY: HUMILITY, SMALL SIZE.` · then, large: `HUMILITY FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the apology you owe. Sit still and let the past week drift by: a sharp word, a late reply, a promise that slipped. Don't go hunting for big guilt. Look for one small thing where you were the doer and it wasn't right. When you find it, say the words silently, plainly, with no but on the end: I'm sorry. Feel how short the sentence is. The bell holds the time.
Mithat neevee, sweetness and lowness. Humility as the doorway: while I am the doer blocks it, nothing else comes through.
Your line: humility first. Today, say sorry once, out loud, to the person you owe it to, and stop after the word sorry. Day four hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib read the twelfth ashtpadi's warnings about the I that claims to be the doer, and in many gurdwaras Asa di Var, with its line on sweetness and humility, is sung each morning.

pairs: a morning hymn sung in gurdwaras

myth: in Sikh teaching, humility is meant to feel grim and sour
Guru Nanak pairs it with sweetness: mithat neevee.
the twelfth ashtpadi says peace can't come while I am the doer
the I in the doorway blocks everything else.
the twelfth ashtpadi is the last of Sukhmani
Sukhmani has twenty-four; the twelfth sits near the middle.

fork.setup: you snapped at a friend. you want to apologize. which version fits the twelfth ashtpadi?
options: I'm sorry, but you started it.
fork.reveal: the plain one. the but defends the self, which is pride's job; owning it lets the I step out of the doorway.

original.note: Gurmukhi: mithat neevee, sweetness and humility, from Guru Nanak's Asa di Var.

trapdoor: what you thought: humility is one virtue among many.
what it means: humility is the doorway; while the I claims to be the doer, nothing else gets in.
what a scholar hears: Asa di Var calls sweetness and humility the essence (tat) of virtues, and Sukhmani 12's second stanza ties the doer-I to the round of births.
